Nov 12th 2026
Russia and Ukraine held their first peace negotiations in nine months. The talks, brokered by America and held in Abu Dhabi, ended with no big breakthrough, though both sides agreed to swap more prisoners of war. Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump’s envoys, then flew to Moscow, to try to persuade Vladimir Putin to include other European countries in future negotiations. They also prepared to meet Volodymyr Zelensky. Ukraine is wary about a meeting between Mr Trump, Mr Putin and Xi Jinping, which Mr Putin is seeking to use to discuss an end to the conflict, but without Mr Zelensky.
France accused Iran’s revolutionary guards of being behind a spate of cyber-attacks on the food-refrigeration systems of big supermarkets. In mid-October the hackers tapped into the supermarkets’ cooling systems, which can be controlled over the internet, damaging goods worth tens of millions of euros and raising concerns about an attack on food security. Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, blamed Iran, describing it as an act of “unprecedented aggressiveness”.
In Spain unions held their first national strike in 14 years to protest against the high cost of housing, a big issue in the general election that has been called for November 29th. The ruling Socialists are currently trailing in the polls.
A 24-year-old man shot dead six people in Krakow, Poland’s second-biggest city. He is also suspected of killing his parents and sister. The incident shocked Poland, where gun crime is rare. The perpetrator, who was shot by police and eventually died from his wounds, was described as a loner. It is unclear what his motives were. Ministers suggested he was inspired by far-right ideology, a claim that was disputed by conservatives.
An attempt by a Republican congressman to impeach Pete Hegseth, America’s secretary of war, failed after other Republicans moved to defeat it. Thomas Massie, who lost his primary election in May to a Trumpier candidate, brought several charges against Mr Hegseth relating to the Iran war. Holding a rare press conference, Mr Hegseth defended his record and described the impeachment attempt as a farce. Democrats looked on in glee and vowed to revive the proceedings next year.
Trying to regain the initiative after the Republicans’ stinging defeat in the midterms, Donald Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff. The combative Mr Miller has advised the president on policy during his first and second terms, pushing for harsh immigration measures and deadly strikes against alleged drug-traffickers in the Caribbean, among other things.
Scott Colom was declared the winner in Mississippi’s Senate election, becoming the first black person to represent the state in the Senate since the post-civil-war era. He is also the first Democrat from Mississippi to be elected to the Senate since 1982. Counting continued in Alaska’s close Senate race, where the Democrat holds a narrow lead over the Republican.
Meanwhile, as the Republicans prepare to become the minority party in Congress, Republican senators re-elected John Thune to continue as their leader in the Senate. In the House of Representatives Republicans chose Jim Jordan, a vocal Trump supporter, to lead them. Mike Johnson, the current speaker, decided not to stand.
California’s ballot proposal for a billionaires’ tax appears to have failed, though the result is not yet official. Proposition 40 attracted support from unions and progressives, including Bernie Sanders, a senator from Vermont. It was opposed by Silicon Valley and Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, who said it would cause entrepreneurs to flee the state.
An American soldier was arrested in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia. He reportedly worked at a NATO base. Meanwhile, American military aircraft were withdrawn from a second air-force base in Britain, according to reports, amid heightened security over a possible attack from Iran. American planes flew out of RAF Mildenhall and relocated elsewhere. In September American bombers were redeployed from RAF Fairford because of a potential Iranian plot. America’s Justice Department has laid charges against three alleged operatives for Iran, including in that case.
China’s carbon emissions fell by 3.1% year on year in the third quarter, the biggest quarterly decline since the covid pandemic. The Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a Finnish think-tank, said lower coal and oil consumption helped bring emissions for the first nine months down by 0.5%.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation as vice-president of Indonesia , following court rulings that there was no evidence of his graduating from high school, and he was thus ineligible to stand in the 2024 election. Mr Gibran is the son of Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, who was president until 2024. Relations between Jokowi and the current president, Prabowo Subianto, have soured amid claims that Jokowi’s allies in the administration wiretapped Mr Prabowo’s phone.
In Bangladesh supporters of Sheikh Hasina clashed with police. The former prime minister fled the country in 2024 amid widespread protests. She lives in exile in India but wants to return to Bangladesh in December, even though she has been sentenced to death in absentia for her brutal crackdown on the protesters. The Bangladeshi government refuses to issue her a passport.
There was no clear winner in New Zealand’s election. The final results will not be announced until the end of the month, but Christopher Luxon, the centre-right prime minister and leader of the National Party, is talking to the centrist Opportunity Party about joining his coalition.
Isaac Herzog, Israel’s president, asked Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the centrist Yashar party, to form a new government . A majority of members in the newly elected Knesset endorsed Mr Eisenkot, but the opposition parties did not agree on the composition of the new coalition. Mr Eisenkot indicated that he wanted to form a minority “emergency” government, without either Arab or ultra-Orthodox parties. He will have up to six weeks to convince his partners.
Seasonal flooding swamped Gaza, drenching the tents of around 350,000 people. In unusual criticism, Donald Trump’s Board of Peace warned Israeli politicians that aid provisions are “insufficient” and urged them to let more supplies into the strip.
Paraguay’s parliament removed Santiago Peña as president amid a scandal that led to the collapse of a popular bank and caused the head of the central bank to step down. Mr Peña, who had offered to resign, was placed under house arrest amid allegations that he used his influence to direct government work towards the bank; Mr Peña used to hold shares in a company tied to it. He denies any wrongdoing.
Pope Leo visited Latin America, just a month after cancer surgery. The pontiff started off in Uruguay and then headed to Argentina, where 2.5m people attended one mass. In a televised address attended by Javier Milei, the pope criticised the president’s austerity programme because of its impact on the poor. He then went to Peru, where he worked for over 20 years as a missionary before taking the top job in the Vatican. At least 3m people turned out to greet him in what he describes as his homeland.

Nov 12th 2026
Nvidia was engulfed in turmoil after Jensen Huang , the chipmaker’s chief executive, admitted to having an extramarital affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean cloud-computing company that buys Nvidia’s hardware. American officials suspect the woman is a Chinese agent and that Megaspeed helps China bypass export controls on American chips. The affair has raised questions about whether Nvidia intervened to thwart a government investigation into Megaspeed last year. Donald Trump said the FBI had started an inquiry. As reports surfaced that Mr Huang also had an affair with an executive at Nvidia, the board deliberated over removing him.
Nvidia’s share price plunged in reaction to the news about Mr Huang, unsettling already jittery investors. Chip stocks recently recorded one of their worst days ever, which saw the NASDAQ 100 drop by around 6%. The sell-off came on the heels of the Democrats’ victory in the midterms; the party has pledged to curb the construction of data centres and so slow investment in AI. Stock markets had clawed back some of their losses over subsequent days, though investors remain cautious. Markets in Japan and South Korea also sank.
Investors took some comfort from CoreWeave’s latest earnings, which suggested that its sales remain strong. CoreWeave is one of the neoclouds, a group of fast-growing companies that buy specialist AI chips and rent them out, but are also laden with debt. In October stock markets swooned when CoreWeave raised the prospect of taking on even more debt.
A former employee at OpenAI’s headquarters pleaded not guilty to spying. Prosecutors allege that the man, a Saudi national, had frequent contact with an unnamed member of Saudi Arabia’s royal family.
An updated filing with regulators indicated that Anthropic could be worth $1.4trn at its forthcoming IPO, making it one of the biggest ever. Reports suggest that the huge demand for shares in the firm may actually see its value head towards $1.5trn. The stock is expected to start trading on November 19th.
SoftBank booked a $3.7bn charge against its data-centre investments in America, driving it to its first quarterly net loss in two years. The charge was reportedly related to energy equipment, including gas turbines SoftBank had reserved to power the data centres. Unable to use all the energy SoftBank apparently decided to write off the contracts.
Alibaba confirmed that its subsidiary chips business, T-Head, has filed for an IPO in Hong Kong. T-Head lies at the centre of Alibaba’s thrust into AI and computing; in September it released its next-generation processor. The details of the stock-market listing haven’t been decided yet, but it should enable T-Head to raise its own capital in the markets.
America’s monthly inflation rate was 0.4% in October, more than markets were expecting (the Bureau of Labour Statistics did not calculate an annual rate because the government was shut down in the corresponding month last year). Investors are now all but certain that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates again in December. Speaking ahead of the latest inflation data Christopher Waller, a Fed governor, suggested the central bank may need to lift its benchmark rate by half a percentage point.
Clare Lombardelli, a member of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee, said that unless inflationary pressures weaken, interest rates may rise again “in the near term”. The bank recently increased its base rate for the first time in more than three years, lifting it to 4%.
Britain’s economy expanded by 1.9% in the third quarter compared with the same period a year earlier. The Office for National Statistics said this was almost entirely due to strong growth in the services sector.
The value of China’s goods exports surged by 35% year on year in October, as the country continued to pump out chips and AI-related products. China’s cumulative trade surplus for 2026 surpassed $1trn in October, reaching the milestone a month earlier than it did last year.
Skydance outlined the cost savings it expects to achieve from its takeover of Warner Bros. The film-and-TV company expects to save at least $6bn net over the next three years by reducing management layers, scaling AI workflows and streamlining marketing, among other things. The company is already offering voluntary buy-outs to employees ahead of official lay offs.
Elon Musk announced on X that Tesla would be “winding down production of the Cybertruck” from the middle of next year in order to increase output of its robotaxi, the Cybercab. It was unclear if that meant the Cybertruck is being phased out completely. Sales of the futuristic-looking pickup truck, more Terminator than Dukes of Hazzard, have been poor and it has faced several recalls.

Could the news be much more dramatic? Artificial-intelligence models keep growing more powerful, faster than almost anyone predicted. Next week Anthropic, a frontier model-maker, is expected to list its shares in what could be the biggest-ever IPO of an AI firm. Yet in some ways the AI boom is looking wobbly. A sex-and-spying scandal is rocking Nvidia , the top chipmaker. America’s Democratic Party, having won the midterms, is raring to go after data centres and Trump-adjacent tech titans. Some fear an almighty tech bust is coming. How worried should the world be?
History offers clues. Plenty of past technologies, from canals and railways to the internet, have brought market euphoria and then despair. Bets on them went wrong even though the underlying technologies proved revolutionary.
Even techno-optimists like The Economist should worry about a crunch today. The scale of expected investment in AI is vast, an annual average of 3.6% of America’s GDP between 2025 and 2032, by one forecast. AI-related shares have had a dizzying run: the top ten heavily AI-exposed stocks are now nearly 40% of America’s S&P 500 index. Corporate equities have reached 38% of American household net worth—nearly a quarter higher than at the peak of the dotcom boom. And over the 12 months to August net foreign inflows into American equities crossed $1trn for the first time, many times greater than for the entire 2010s.
Jitters over whether all this is sustainable have left stocks roughly flat over six months. After the midterms the NASDAQ index of tech firms fell by 5.5% in a day, as investors fretted that Democrats would block data centres. The share price of Nvidia, whose balance-sheet underpins much of the AI industry, is down by nearly 30% from its peak. When Anthropic floats, bears argue, its prospects will be visible to all in its stock price, a fall in which could trigger a market-wide rout. Anthropic and its main rival, OpenAI, are the customer-facing companies feeding the entire AI supply chain, including data centres, chip designers and chipmakers. If they have too few sales or cannot charge high enough prices, disaster looms.
For investors to have overestimated revenues from AI would be a mistake consistent with financial history. The good news is that the consequences this time would probably be manageable. A dotcom-style equity-market crash could happen; a deep financial crisis is much less likely.
In the past, investors who spotted hot new technologies have often been poor forecasters of who will profit from them. “If a farsighted capitalist had been present at Kitty Hawk, he would have done his successors a huge favour by shooting Orville down,” wrote Warren Buffett in 2008, noting the low profitability of airlines. Many who financed the buildout of fibre-optic cable in the 1990s lost their shirts; it was the tech firms that built businesses on that infrastructure that printed money.
It is easy to see how a bust could happen now. Much of Anthropic’s revenue comes from venture-capital-backed AI startups and could dry up in a crunch. America’s model-makers are only about six months ahead of Chinese rivals who, in effect, give away models for nothing. As we report high valuations for Anthropic and OpenAI assume they will draw further ahead of the competition, or develop new business models which exploit their small lead better.
The gloomiest prognosticators, inspired by a prominent book, say that their failure would lead to a crash like the railway bust of 1873—the last time such a huge investment binge, relative to GDP, took place. Then, disappointing returns caused a financial calamity that brought about deflation and the longest American recession on record.
Fortunately the comparison is ill-judged. Most of America’s capital expenditure on AI goes on imported equipment such as chips. The direct exposure of its economy to the boom is therefore much lower—perhaps 0.3% of GDP. An AI crunch would be far worse for Taiwan’s economy (annual growth rate: 14%) than for America’s. Financial conditions are also utterly different now. In the 1870s there was no central bank and the crash was met with contractionary monetary policy rather than the interest-rate cuts that it would trigger today.
The way the AI boom has been financed is also reassuring. The worst crashes—including 1873’s—follow booms that are mostly funded by debt (and it is excessive household credit, not corporate borrowing, that is the reddest flag). True, the AI industry is borrowing to invest far more than it was two or three years ago, when investments were financed overwhelmingly by the vast cashflows of tech behemoths. Yet the accumulated ai capital stock is still mostly equity-financed. The five “hyperscalers” (big owners of AI data centres) have debts and lease commitments worth around 30% of their book value or just 6% of their market value; their legacy businesses are still hugely profitable. Nvidia’s leverage is negligible. AI debt has not pushed lending to America’s nonfinancial sector above its long-run trend, relative to GDP.
What, then, might happen in an AI-caused crash? Households, nursing losses from the stock market, would spend less. Companies that are highly leveraged, including many “neocloud” data-centre startups, could blow up. There might be a shallow American recession, comparable to that of 2001. For things to get much worse, an AI crash would have to coincide with another calamity, such as a bond-market panic or a war. That is possible: several rich countries’ debts are dangerously high and some global leaders are unpredictably belligerent. But for now, it is not the most likely outcome.
What matters more is what happens to the technology itself. Silicon Valley’s titans think they already have the infrastructure they need to build a superintelligence. Some predict that recursive self-improvement—AIs building more powerful AIs without human input—could occur as soon as next year. A furious political backlash could still interrupt the breakneck advance of AI. A financial crash probably won’t. ■

“ThE IMPATIENCE and dissatisfaction among ordinary people are justified,” Nelson Mandela warned his party in 1999. At the time, the African National Congress (anc) utterly dominated South Africa. A generation on, after years of corruption, stagnation and collapsing public services, South Africans have run out of patience entirely. At local elections on November 4th they handed the ruling party its worst-ever result in a nationwide ballot. Though the ANC eked out 31% of all votes, more than any rival, that was less than half of what it recorded in 2004. In the country’s most dynamic places, it did especially badly. It is no longer the largest party in any big city, including Johannesburg, the commercial capital.
This shows that a young, fragile democracy is working. For decades the ANC could count on the votes of black South Africans, who are 80% of the population, because of its role in ending apartheid in 1994. In the early years it also delivered the goods: water, electricity, housing and a safety-net. But over time its performance has flagged. Voters increasingly see the anc as just another party. They punished it for water leaks, power cuts and sewage-ridden streets.
The Democratic Alliance (da), the second-largest party, is now only six percentage points behind the ANC, from almost 50 two decades ago. Previously derided as the “white party”, the da is now the largest party in five of the eight big cities—because it has a record of running cities competently. Depending on coalition negotiations, Helen Zille, a da veteran, could soon become Johannesburg’s first white post-apartheid mayor. You could hardly ask for a more encouraging sign that voters are moving on from racial politics.
Yet there is much to worry about, too. Most South Africans are disillusioned with democracy. Only 35% of possible voters bothered to cast a ballot on November 4th. More than a fifth of black voters opted for black-nationalist parties with ideas that are more Mugabe than Mandela. These include uMkhonto weSizwe (mk), which will probably run Durban, the city with the busiest port in sub-Saharan Africa, and the Economic Freedom Fighters (eff). Dangerous grassroots movements, from anti-migrant vigilantes to white nationalists, pose a threat, too.
To his credit Cyril Ramaphosa, South Africa’s president since 2018, acknowledges that his party is losing support. Other leaders, in Africa and elsewhere, instead rig elections and violently cling to power. Since 2024 at the national level he has led a Government of National Unity, in effect an anc-da coalition, that has brought some political stability and sensible reforms. But his tenure is entering its twilight. He will be replaced as party leader in 2027 and must leave the presidency no later than in 2029. He still has much to do to secure his desired legacy: as the disciple of Mandela who shored up South Africa’s graft-eroded institutions, reformed the economy and thwarted ruinous populism.
An urgent priority for the country is to run its cities better. That requires more local power-sharing among parties, just as they have learned to do nationally. The anc will have to get used to being, at times, a junior coalition partner. Some in the party would prefer to unite the so-called “black parties”, cutting deals with mk and the eff. But that would lead to much worse and more corrupt governance, which voters would soon notice. Smaller parties, like Actionsa, which won 16% of the vote in Johannesburg, also face a test of their seriousness.
A political realignment is under way that brings some risks for the continent’s largest economy. But mostly the change is welcome: voters are rewarding those who govern better, and punishing those who don’t, just as the architects of the constitution hoped they would. When the anc failed to deliver a better life for all, voters looked for an alternative. Mandela would have understood. ■

Editor’s note: Jensen Huang resigned on November 12th.
Jensen Huang is a brilliant man—and a fool. The boss of Nvidia, the world’s leading chip designer and until recently its most valuable company, had an extramarital affair. His lover was an executive at Megaspeed, a little-known cloud-computing firm that has bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia hardware. American officials think she is a Chinese agent, and that her Singapore-based company is a front for smuggling the politically sensitive chips into China.
As we went to press, Nvidia’s board was meeting amid reports that it was planning to oust Mr Huang. If it had yet to find the courage to sack him, fresh allegations of another affair—this time with a direct report—will surely help. His position is untenable, and he must go. The same is true for American officials implicated in the Megaspeed scandal.
Mr Huang’s admission of infidelity on November 8th followed months of rumours about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation). It remains unclear at what point Nvidia’s boss knew that his government thought her to be a Chinese agent, or when the affair ended . Nonetheless, he showed a catastrophic failure of judgment. Romance with a customer creates an obvious conflict of interest. And given his position as the steward of an American technology that China desperately covets, Mr Huang should have been extra wary. Instead, he lied publicly about the nature of their relationship as recently as last month.
If it is true that he also had an affair with a subordinate, no self-respecting board could allow him to remain. And Mr Huang’s transgressions may prove to have been graver still. Questions swirl as to whether Nvidia’s chief counsel intervened last year in an investigation into Megaspeed by America’s Commerce Department, which is responsible for enforcing export controls. Mr Huang’s advocacy of looser chip controls, ostensibly to keep China hooked on American technology, now arouses suspicion, as does his championing of Chinese open-source models.
Those who have argued that Mr Huang should stay reason that he is essential to Nvidia, and that Nvidia is essential to America’s lead over China in AI. Yet it is precisely because Nvidia is so important that he cannot continue as its chief executive. It is in America’s long-term interests that there be penalties for egregious misconduct at the top of firms which are crucial to national security. And for all Mr Huang’s undoubted brilliance, the interests of Nvidia’s shareholders would hardly be served by a scandal-ridden chief executive facing a merry-go-round of investigations, including by the FBI.
That there is no obvious successor makes the board’s job unenviable, but not impossible. Mr Huang has been deeply involved in every aspect of his business, with as many as 60 executives reporting to him directly—a situation the board should not have allowed. No one has been prepared for the top job. Even so, an experienced executive such as Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief, should be capable of stepping in to stabilise the business while a permanent successor, perhaps from outside, is appointed.
Mr Huang is not the only one to have shown dismal judgment in the Megaspeed debacle. The Commerce Department, under Howard Lutnick, has failed abjectly to stem the flow of America’s best chips to China. It appears to have allowed Nvidia to keep selling to Megaspeed even after concerns over smuggling were raised, and to have resisted calls by the Pentagon, the Treasury and others in the administration to blacklist the Singaporean firm. Like Mr Huang, Mr Lutnick has advocated weaker chip-export controls.
Alas, the secretary of commerce is unlikely to resign. But as Democrats take control of Congress, they will interrogate not only Mr Lutnick but also President Donald Trump, who has bought Nvidia shares and tapped the company to fund his new ballroom. For two years incoherent policy and lax enforcement have allowed China to gain ground in the race for a technology that may prove more powerful than nuclear weapons. With luck, that will now change.
For years Mr Huang has been courted by governments and treated as a rock star. Like many powerful leaders, including others in Silicon Valley, he came to believe that he was too important for the normal rules to apply to him. The same attitude can be found, in even larger doses, within the Trump administration. This culture of impunity must end. It has damaged one of America’s great corporate successes and undermined its national security. After Mr Huang's, other heads should roll, too. ■
Clarification (November 11th): An earlier version of this article mentioned that Cantor Fitzgerald, an investment bank run by Howard Lutnick’s sons, holds a large position in Nvidia. That stake reflects its asset-management and other activities on behalf of clients.

THE CLIMATE does not care where the carbon dioxide accumulating in the atmosphere comes from. It simply takes note of how much there is and dispenses weather accordingly.
The humans who have to live with that changing weather need to take a slightly more nuanced view. Less carbon dioxide being emitted is good. Less carbon dioxide being emitted because of structural change—change that should decrease emissions further in years to come—is better.
According to the Global Carbon Budget, a consortium that monitors the carbon cycle, carbon-dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will fall by 0.4% in 2026. That compares with an average rise of 0.8% a year over the past seven years. The fall is driven in large part by decreases in Chinese emissions . These, as we report in the China section, have been dropping all year. In the third quarter they fell by 3.1% year-on-year, the largest such fall since the covid lockdowns.
Those assembled in Antalya, Turkey for the UN’s annual climate summit, COP31, would doubtless love to see this happy circumstance as an outcome of their unceasing efforts. Dream on. The principal reason is that the foolhardy war with Iran launched by America and Israel has pumped up the price of oil and natural gas. When fuel becomes more expensive, people burn less of it, and carbon emissions fall.
Normally such changes get reset when prices subside and consumption rebounds. This time that should happen less. If your response to expensive petrol is buying an electric vehicle, rather than driving fewer miles in your existing car, then your need to buy petrol has been cut whether or not it becomes cheap again. And a lot of people are buying EVs, both in China and elsewhere; petrol-powered cars now account for less than half of all new-car sales worldwide.
Another reason for the drop in Chinese emissions is that the generosity with which the state has treated makers of solar panels and wind turbines is paying off. China is getting more and more terawatt-hours from wind and solar, both because more kit has been installed and because grids are better at getting what is generated to where it is wanted. Growth in renewable-electricity generation has outstripped growth in total electricity demand; emissions from coal-fired power are down.
The industrial policy that has made renewables cheap in China has done the same for the world at large—as long as it buys Chinese. Throughout South-East Asia and in much of Africa, Chinese solar panels and batteries are replacing diesel generators and eating into the revenues of national grids. They are also providing the huge advantages of electrified life to people previously denied them—all without adding to emissions.
None of this was done specifically for the benefit of those exposed to the hazards of climate change. The main reasons have been industrial policy, economic policy and a quest for energy independence. Since these motives remain strong, emissions may continue to fall.
To speed up the process, policymakers should amplify the changes already happening and keep up pressure on non-carbon-dioxide emissions. There are some reasons to be careful about importing cheap Chinese clean tech, which include worries about back doors in the software that they rely on. In general, though, if past Chinese subsidies are offering the world technologies to generate cheap power and help with the climate, do not let protectionism spoil a good thing.
Also, governments should do what they can to encourage the switch to electricity. Enabling power prices to vary as much as possible by location and time of day would keep overall costs down. Encouraging the replacement of things which burn fossil fuels—cars, boilers and the like—with technologies that achieve the same goals electrically, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, is also wise.
Electrification is not the be-all and end-all of climate policy. Making a stable climate possible requires more. Not everything can be plugged in; not all systems can be made entirely fossil-free. A deeply damaging degree of climate change remains plausible. But the clearest path to avoiding it is a world in which the trends driving electrification are given free rein and a following wind. ■

TWO TYPES of movie stand out in America’s box-office revival this year. The first is indie fare such as “Obsession” and “Backrooms”, made by two YouTubers who spent peanuts on films that grossed over $920m between them. The second is extravaganzas like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “The Odyssey”, which cost hundreds of millions of dollars and grossed a combined $4.3bn. Such extremes reflect a new topography of Hollywood: the twin peaks of lo-fi creator content and hi-fi premium stuff. As with the rest of show business, anything stuck in the middle is in trouble.
On one extreme sits YouTube , Hollywood’s most potent disruptive force. As we report it has become America’s dominant TV platform, with a share of streaming almost as big as those of Netflix, Skydance and Walt Disney combined. Its business model makes it easy to spend on content, since it pays according to performance rather than buying shows up front, as legacy studios do. Its creators, the best of whom are superstars in their own right, upload an average of 20m videos a day. In an indirect form of flattery, streamers such as Netflix are poaching them.
On the other extreme is content so lavishly produced that watching it is an event in its own right. Take America’s top two blockbusters. They generated about a fifth of all box-office revenues this year; some IMAX tickets for “The Odyssey” sold out a year in advance. Sport and live entertainment also fit the bill. Last year 96 of America’s top 100 telecasts were sports-related.
Lo-fi is a volume play. Hi-fi is a value one. But they have something in common: human connection. YouTube’s creators establish an intimacy with their audiences, born of years of fandom. Driving people to glitzier fare is the thrill of sharing something special, such as the spectacle of the imax or the tension of the Super Bowl. Such experiences need not cost megabucks. A24, an independent studio, has mastered the art of making people not only watch its films but talk about them. Even one of its documentaries—Nathan Fielder’s “You Can See Everything”—is close to blockbuster status.
Each peak is relatively AI-proof. Owned by Google, YouTube offers AI tools to creators. It is the biggest distribution platform for AI-made video content. At the other end, people watch World Cup football matches, and perhaps also films like “The Odyssey”, precisely because they are triumphs of human endeavour. This makes them hard for bots to copy.
Unfortunately most show business lies between Hollywood’s two peaks. For years studio executives have made a virtue of offering all things to all people—with mixed financial results. Skydance, newly created by the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros, two Hollywood studios, is a case in point. Its two streaming platforms, HBO Max and Paramount Plus, cater respectively to film buffs and middle America. Its 50 cable channels range from CNN to the Food Network. Its sports rights straddle American football and tennis. From next year onwards, to satisfy one of the antitrust conditions of the merger, it aims to churn out a new film every fortnight or so. A similar spray-and-pray approach is common across mainstream music, gaming and publishing.
Combine all Skydance’s broadcast, cable and streaming services, and they still draw less attention than YouTube. Bundle together HBO and Paramount Plus, as planned early next year, and they will still be less than half the size of Netflix. As for producing upscale movies, it would be easier if Skydance’s acquisition spree had not saddled it with $87bn of debt.
Netflix may be big enough to survive as a stand-alone streamer. Disney is buoyed by its theme parks. Skydance looks stuck in the mid-size trap. It could join forces with the American arm of TikTok, part-owned by Oracle, to counter YouTube (the chairmen of Oracle and Skydance are father and son). It could use AI to cut operating costs and invest more in premium films and TV. What it cannot do is muddle through. The valley between the peaks is a dangerous place to be. ■

Britain’s ban on some pornography is based on flimsy evidence, you said, and you questioned the basis of the new offences that have just come into force (“Gagging order”, November 7th). As the author of the government’s independent review of pornography, I approached the task with an open mind. Academic literature was reviewed and I heard extensive evidence from researchers, regulators, abuse charities, safeguarding professionals, police officers, teachers, parents and young people. MUCH OF THE debate about artificial intelligence, including a recent leader in The Economist, asks how to prevent a powerful new technology from making the world more dangerous. There is an equally important, more urgent question: how quickly can we use it to make an already dangerous world safer?
The world that large language models entered was very vulnerable. In 2017 NotPetya, a Russian cyber-attack aimed at Ukraine, spread worldwide within hours, deleting data and paralysing systems, including those of Maersk, which carries about a fifth of global shipping. In 2023 Iranian-linked hackers broke into American water utilities, forcing operators to switch to manual control. More worrying still are the attacks not yet triggered: Chinese state hackers have planted footholds in American power, water and transport systems, ready to strike silently during a conflict.
Few of these attacks relied on brilliant new exploits—code that weaponises systems’ flaws to cause harm. They succeeded because the defenders could not find, fix or fence off known weaknesses fast enough across sprawling, ageing systems. The cost of that status quo belongs in any honest accounting of AI risk.
I have worked on both sides of cyber-conflict: conducting intelligence operations at America’s National Security Agency, then running its Cybersecurity Directorate to turn those lessons into defences. Later, at the White House, I pushed through the first mandatory cyber-security rules for America’s pipelines, railways and airports. The experience taught me something important: AI can help defenders even more than it can help attackers.
True, AI makes the challenge harder in some ways. It lowers the skill needed by attackers, and lets them jiggle every digital door-knob, continuously and at scale. It is already speeding up the discovery of new flaws, including in software foundational to the internet. But the old rule of cyber-conflict, that defenders must be strong everywhere while attackers need to find only one weakness, rested on defenders lacking the time, people and money to cover everything. AI alleviates that problem.
AI is already making defenders’ response to these threats stronger. They own their code and can task AI to pre-emptively analyse it line by line from all possible angles of attack, rather than probing it only from the outside as attackers must do. They see their own network traffic, so AI can spot the subtle signs of an intruder using stolen credentials and legitimate tools, as China’s hackers do, which older tools miss.
Using AI available today, utilities can turn operational data into virtual replicas of power grids and water systems. These “digital twins” let operators test defences without putting essential services at risk. Attackers, working from outside, can build only crude approximations.
Crucially, AI can fix flaws after finding them. In DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge last year, AI systems scanning open-source software of the kind that underpins critical infrastructure patched 43 planted vulnerabilities, and uncovered 18 previously unknown flaws, fixing 11 of them. For ageing equipment that cannot safely be patched, AI can give each flaw a specific workaround, such as a firewall rule or a settings change, tested on a digital twin before it goes live. And AI is cheap enough that small, under-staffed utilities can use it too.
None of this happens by default. AI favours defenders only if they move with urgency. Governments should start with the infrastructure operators and shared suppliers whose failure would cause the greatest disruption, enlisting AI labs to find flaws in their code or firmware and produce fixes by set deadlines. Governments should share the cost for smaller operators. Success should be measured by how quickly threats are contained and whether essential services survive an attack. Critical-infrastructure operators could address the highest-priority systems within a year, judging by how quickly they met the cyber-security standards issued by the Biden administration.
Findings should be shared with trusted partners using the co-ordinated-disclosure practices that keep fixes from tipping off attackers before systems are patched. The aim should be for a discovery in one country to strengthen every country running the same technology.
Such practical partnerships are more urgent than AI treaties, and the foundations exist. NATO’s annual Locked Shields exercise brings together thousands of participants from dozens of countries to defend power grids, water systems and other networks against live attacks. The exercises could be expanded to include using AI to generate patches and controls, sharing the results across the alliance.
Here, too, there is precedent. In 2021 America formed the International Counter Ransomware Initiative, now made up of nearly 70 countries. Members share threat warnings and forensic techniques, including how to trace ransoms laundered through the crypto ecosystem. They co-ordinate policy; for example, by pledging not to pay ransoms. Alongside law-enforcement takedowns of gangs and their money-laundering networks, the effort has squeezed the business: after peaking at over $1bn in 2023, ransom payments have fallen each year since.
The time has come to use AI as aggressively on defence as adversaries will use it in attack. A serious international agenda for AI safety should explain not only how it will contain the risks of a new technology, but how it will keep the lights on for the world’s citizens, and how soon. ■
Anne Neuberger is a general partner and the head of global affairs at Andreessen Horowitz. She previously served as Deputy National Security Adviser of the United States.

Both artificial intelligence and the tricky business of valuing stocks boil down to questions of timelines. Establishing what a company is worth is a hazy exercise at the best of times, full of courageous assumptions about which cashflows will arrive when. Consider, too, timelines for AI—the years, few or many, until the technology’s capabilities surpass humans’—and the exercise veers into incoherence.
Markets do not enjoy the luxury of coherence, though. Take the imminent listing of Anthropic, the first big pure-play AI developer to go public. Anthropic’s prospectus touts the many remarkable (and profitable) ways in which advanced AI could transform the economy, but also warns would-be buyers off. “Our decision-making may run counter to investors’ expectations,” it says, for instance with “forward investments…that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance”.
Still, somewhere between Utopia and Armageddon, investors need to find a way to pick a number. Anthropic is aiming to float at a valuation of around $1.5trn, which would make it one of the 15 biggest public companies in the world.
The listing comes at a precarious time for AI. Jitters about data-centre debt collided with midterm elections in America, where AI-sceptical candidates prevailed, and, bizarrely, with the revelation that Jensen Huang , the boss of the chipmaker Nvidia, was having an affair with an alleged Chinese agent.
Before all that, Anthropic looked set for a valuation of $2trn or more (see chart 1). OpenAI, its main rival, has punted its own listing into next year. Nvidia’s share price was about 30% below its recent peak as The Economist went to press. The “neoclouds”, which borrow, often prodigiously, to run data centres, have done worse. But a comeback may be on. Shares in CoreWeave, one of the largest, rose by 25% on November 11th, following strong earnings. The stock had previously been down two-thirds from its high point this year in May. And Anthropic’s IPO is, reportedly, heavily oversubscribed.
So the IPO will be a weighty moment. However many trillions Anthropic lists at, from then on it—and, increasingly, AI more widely—will be judged not with the gauzy optimism of venture capitalists but with the beady eyes of Wall Street. Investors will wonder whether the technology can possibly generate enough cash to justify these valuations or underwrite the colossal scale of data-centre construction planned over the next few years.
The numbers are vast. The Economist calculates that AI needs around $3trn in revenue by 2030 for the planned data-centre buildout to offer a conventional rate of return. Other analysts, including Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of Columbia Business School and a duo at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, have reached similar figures. To put that number into perspective, all compensation for all workers—wages, plus perks like health insurance—adds up to around $16.5trn in America, or $35trn across the OECD, a club mostly of rich countries. So AI would need to lay claim to almost a tenth of today’s rich-world wages for the data-centre boom to pencil out. Of course, that could happen in a more benign fashion if the entire economy grows swiftly—and AI evangelists do also expect dramatic growth from here.
Safe to say, AI isn’t quite there yet. Anthropic has reported that its annualised run-rate revenue at the end of October was $81bn. OpenAI’s was $50bn as of the end of September. Toss in smaller developers, as well as Google’s, Meta’s and Microsoft’s revenues from their own models, and the AI model-makers might be generating around $200bn in total.
All that cash sits at the top of a funnel, cascading downward into the rest of the ecosystem—keeping other AI businesses afloat and persuading investors to hand them more money. The models that Anthropic, OpenAI and the others sell must be run on chips, most often designed by Nvidia and manufactured by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Those chips in turn rely on a bevy of components. A shortage of one, RAM, a type of memory, sent the stocks of the main South Korean memory-makers, Samsung and SK Hynix, soaring in the spring. Those chips must then be housed in a data centre, festooned with further complicated electronics. All that needs electricity to power it, too: a windfall for the makers of gas turbines, which generate much of the electricity behind the AI boom. Everything in AI-world, in other words, relies on revenue at the top of that funnel continuing to flow in, ideally at an ever-increasing rate.
Getting from $200bn to $3trn means a leap of an order of magnitude (or an OOM, in Silicon Valley-speak). Could that happen? Because so many of the largest players in AI have been privately held, tracing the exact path of their revenues is tricky. But the previous OOM did not take long. The combined revenues of Anthropic, OpenAI and a number of smaller developers (but not Google, Meta and so on) probably crossed $10bn around March of 2025. Today, that figure is $130bn.
The next leap will be tougher. One cause of AI’s recent wobble was a fear that revenue growth may be slowing. Alternative-data proxies like Ramp, which tracks AI spending on company credit cards, and TickerTrends, which collates data such as social-media posts and spending patterns from panels of businesses and consumers, point to slowing revenue growth among the AI developers. A model fitting those data sets to the revenue figures that Anthropic, OpenAI and others have released suggests three-month revenue growth slowed from 80-90% in the spring to 12% in October (see chart 2).
By usual standards, even the smallest of those numbers reflects extraordinarily rapid gains. And not every proxy is gloomy; figures from OpenRouter, a tool which helps developers switch AI providers, now show spending on Anthropic’s, OpenAI‘s and Google’s models surging out of an earlier funk. Still, the more that revenue growth tapers off, the further out of reach the next OOM may slip. Once Anthropic and, eventually, OpenAI list, the reporting requirements of public markets will make any such slowdown far easier to spot.
A trillion-dollar AI economy would change the world, in a way that today’s hundred-billion-dollar one has not. Right now, the technology’s economic impact is still limited outside the AI sector itself. Profit margins and revenue per employee have surged at the “Magnificent Seven” tech giants, but are close to flat for the “S&P 493”, the rest of America’s benchmark S&P 500 index of big companies. Software stocks have now largely rebounded from the clobbering they took at the start of the year, during the “SaaSpocalypse”, when investors worried that automated coding would make it easy to cheaply duplicate nearly any software product.
Macroeconomic figures also have not moved much. Productivity growth has been strong in America, but not much stronger of late than in the early 2020s. Meanwhile, it remains painfully slow elsewhere in the rich world, even in countries like Britain whose firms have adopted AI at a similar pace to America. Global bond markets also do not seem to be pricing in all that dramatic an uplift to growth.
So far the only profession truly upended by AI is software engineering. Many coders now hardly touch code themselves; instead, they supervise armies of AI agents. America’s “information” sector, which includes software publishing, has the highest and fastest-growing AI penetration rate in the economy, according to figures from the US Census Bureau (see chart 3). Mercor, an AI-data company, claims to spend more on AI agents than on employee salaries.
That is extreme, but not entirely unrepresentative. Tech companies’ AI spending looks nothing like the rest. The average VC-backed company spends around $100 per employee per month on AI, according to data from Ramp (see chart 4). Regular firms spend only $10 or so. Many, after a wave of “tokenmaxxing” AI enthusiasm, are becoming more cautious. In October Goldman Sachs, a bank, banned non-engineers from using AI coding tools, citing disappointing productivity gains and concerns about cyber-security risk. (Though JPMorgan, a rival, has since announced that it is doubling down on the technology.)
Where tremendous gains have been most visible is in the underlying capabilities of AI models. A report by METR, a non-profit outfit that embedded researchers at Anthropic, found the pace of improvement in Anthropic’s models may well have doubled in the past year. Recent months have brought a drumbeat of announcements of AI solutions to unsolved mathematics problems, or novel AI-enabled cyber-attacks.
But the surging investment in training AI models has also meant that each leap in model intelligence has been more expensive than the last. That raises the commercial imperative still further to deploy this intelligence profitably.
For now, selling access to AI has been an excellent business. Improvements have arrived fast enough, and the best models have been appealing enough, to let developers charge healthy margins. Anthropic’s gross margin in this year’s first half was 85%. At first glance, then, AI might remind investors of the previous generation of runaway software success stories.
But in their fundamental economics, AI and conventional software are quite different businesses. Software products, from software-as-a-service tools like Salesforce to Google to the social-networking giants, had several appealing characteristics from an investor’s perspective. Switching to a competitor was costly, so their moats were wide. Users would have to relearn how to use a complex tool from scratch. Network effects benefited the biggest players and stymied upstarts: why join a social-media site with no other users, or an ad network with few prospective customers? And, once the software was built, it was cheap to distribute. So, the bigger a company’s customer base, the more users it could spread its fixed costs across, and the tougher any rival would find it to compete on price.
Selling AI models has, so far, been something like the reverse. Switching is trivial. For developers, tools like OpenRouter make it as simple as changing a line of code. For consumers, one chatbot looks much like another. Many products, like Cursor, a coding agent, offer a drop-down menu to toggle between different model providers. Others like Instinct, a personal-assistant agent, make even that decision invisible by juggling among models on the back end, balancing performance and costs. And the cost of serving a new customer is not near-zero, as with regular software. Each new query must be run in an expensive data centre, on a scarce chip.
Still, Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s pricing power has held up thus far. Breakneck revenue growth relies on that position lasting. The firms can manage that either by continuing to make their current business model work, or by finding new ones. They are trying both. So far, though switching costs are low, users have been willing to pay a premium for the best models. But at the current pace of development, each gets only a narrow window, weeks or at most months, to recoup its training costs before a successor surpasses it.
Will cheaper models become a threat? Once a certain level of model intelligence is achieved, it tends to be commodified and plummet in price (see chart 5). That reflects competition between American AI players as well as the threat of Chinese fast-followers. Today’s best Chinese offering on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which aggregates a wide range of AI benchmarks, is Kimi K3.1 Pro, which scores around the same as GPT 5.5 Pro from OpenAI, which was the strongest publicly available American model just over six months ago, in April. Over the past few years, Chinese models have been consistently about that far behind.
Cheap models could be especially worrying if trained cleverly. Researchers at Bridgewater, a hedge fund, using tools from Thinking Machines, an AI startup, found that a small fine-tuned Chinese model beat the then-leading models from Anthropic and OpenAI at processing financial documents. Such fine-tuning requires investments in data and computing that only big firms will deem worthwhile, but if the finding holds more broadly, it will be a tempting way to lower the AI bill.
Still, some uses of AI will always demand the absolute best, especially those that are adversarial, like trading or cyber-security. There, success means staying ahead of rivals. And in other cases too it may be worth paying a premium. Large unsupervised swarms of AI agents, of the sort that OpenAI accidentally set loose to hack Hugging Face, an AI startup, earlier this year, still need top-flight intelligence.
The big developers’ lead on capabilities also could grow. The computational power needed to train the latest models is becoming a moat, keeping upstarts out. Chinese developers are constrained by a (thus far) smaller data-centre buildout and American restrictions on chip sales to China. And Anthropic says that it is getting better at impeding distillation, the process where less capable models are trained on the output of better ones, which has helped Chinese firms stay in the race on the cheap.
AI developers could find ways to shift their business to make spending stickier. In recent months Anthropic and OpenAI have announced a crop of specialist tools for law, science and finance. Anthropic has also set up a joint venture with Blackstone, a private-equity firm, Goldman Sachs and others to start selling bespoke AI services to businesses. Each is an effort to find revenue streams where the company can embed itself and dig a deeper moat.
But AI products can only ever be so sticky. By making computers easier to use, and more responsive to human-language requests, AI itself has simplified the process of moving from provider to provider. Anthropic cannily capitalised on this fact earlier this year, when its spat with the Pentagon drove a wave of sympathetic switchers from ChatGPT. Upon setting up Claude, users were given a prompt that they could paste into ChatGPT, asking the rival model to summarise what it knew about them. Claude would then digest the output, and be able to offer personalised responses from the get-go.
Another option for the model companies is proprietary trading. This could be of the literal sort. Nearly every rumour imaginable has been attached at some point to Safe Superintelligence, the secretive AI-research company run by Ilya Sutskever, a former chief scientist of OpenAI. A popular, if barmy, one is that it is using its models for high-frequency trading. A more likely version of that business model for Anthropic and its peers is prop trading of the metaphorical variety: monetising AI by using it directly, potentially in a joint venture, in domains like drug development or robotics, where breakthroughs could be highly profitable. For sufficiently smart models, restricting access to a few ultra-high-paying customers, which would also choke off the threat of distillation, could be a shrewder move than a wide release.
Politics could get in the way. America’s midterms were the first big elections where AI was on the ballot, and it fared poorly. Ahead of the results, The Economist found that Americans living near a data-centre site swung towards the Democrats by around five percentage points over the year, compared with voters with the same demographic characteristics elsewhere. Voters opted to restrict data centres in all but one of the 41 local referendums on the topic. Anti-data-centre candidates won stunning victories. Most consequential was the surprise election as governor of Texas of Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat who campaigned for a pause in data-centre construction. Texas is host to around a third of America’s data-centre buildout.
The potential moratoriums would hit projects not yet under way, most of them due in 2028 or beyond. In states that elected governors who support a data-centre pause, there are 25.6 gigawatts’ worth of not-yet-started data centres due in 2028, finds Maya Barkin of SemiAnalysis, a research firm. That is equal to just under half America’s current data-centre capacity.
Still, new data centres are comfortably profitable enough to fund tax cuts and payouts for the communities where they operate. Politicians and developers may well be able to negotiate win-win deals—though that may be easier in places with more Republican voters, who are a little less opposed to data centres. Ms Hinojosa has already toned down her rhetoric. After the election, she clarified that Texas is still pro-business. “It is not that I hate data centres,” she said, though she did accuse the industry of “taking advantage of Texas”.
A bigger risk is federal regulation. None of the proposals floating around Congress with any chance of passing so far would interfere much with the AI developers’ business models. But the new Democratic majority will be keener on regulating AI, and could pivot quickly if, say, a serious cyberattack makes AI risk a top-tier issue.
None of that will stop Anthropic from raising gobsmacking sums. Nor has the buildout of data centres yet shown much sign of slowing. But the business models and political environment that brought AI into the hundreds of billions in revenue won’t carry it into the trillions. For that, the industry will need to adapt and evolve. A looming question is whether Wall Street will have the patience to let it. ■

Seahorse hotels had to be built first. The bony fish off Western Australia’s coasts are bad swimmers, spending most of their lives with their tails hooked around bits of rock, or human artefacts like piers and docks. So when the Royal Australian Navy began to upgrade HMAS Stirling naval base to host nuclear-powered submarines, divers were sent to relocate 263 of the creatures to grids of rebar nearby.
No detail is too small as Australia readies Stirling to host American nuclear-powered attack submarines from next year. That will make it the first American submarine base to be established abroad in half a century, turning it into a port that will project American power deep into Asia. Its site offers a big advantage over America’s existing bases: unlike its one at Guam, it is out of range of all but the most advanced conventional land-based Chinese missiles, but closer to Asian waters than other American submarine bases.
It is also the first big milestone for AUKUS, a deal that was announced five years ago by America, Australia and Britain to jointly design and build nuclear-powered submarines. The American presence at Stirling is part of the first phase, enabling Australian sailors to learn how to sail America’s Virginia-class attack submarines. They will deploy on the boats and maintain them at Stirling. One, USS Colorado, has just arrived at the base for a workover by the Australians, and will return for good at the end of 2027.
In a second phase, Australia is to buy from America and operate its own Virginias in the early 2030s, though there are doubts over whether these will be delivered on time or at all. Finally, Australia and Britain are to jointly design, build and operate a new class of nuclear-powered submarine. The first Australian boat would begin operation in the 2040s. Despite mischief from Chinese spokesmen, no nuclear weapons are involved, only nuclear power. That would let Australian subs range much farther than the country’s current diesel-powered boats without surfacing, giving Australia a punchier deterrent.
AUKUS remains controversial. Much of it was negotiated in secret because Australia was under contract at the time to buy French diesel-powered subs. When that contract was cancelled and AUKUS announced in 2021, it set off a big row. Only afterwards did it become clear to the plotters what a huge challenge it would be. Creaky shipyards in America and Britain would need a big jab of cash to meet the production targets. Some is coming from Australia, which has already handed over $2.6bn of a pledged $6.2bn. That, says Jennifer Parker of the Lowy Institute, a think-tank in Sydney, “is a drop in the bucket compared to what is needed”. But it is a real sign of Australia’s commitment.

But if the cash infusion does not jolt the Anglo-American submarine industrial base out of its torpor, Australia risks ending up with fewer boats than promised. Hence some Australians, particularly those sceptical of the alliance with America, still oppose AUKUS.
But Australia gets quite a bit else out of the deal. In order to share with a new partner the closely held technology used to build and operate nuclear reactors under the oceans, America and Britain have both had to revamp laws and regulations on sharing their most sensitive defence-tech secrets.
